speaker: Patient
text: 54-year-old woman. The patient reports a skin lesion on her right leg that has been present for 1 month. The lesion began as a small red spot and has increased in size. speaker: Doctor
text: Given your history of Crohn's disease and the location of the lesion, I suspect this might be pyoderma gangrenosum rather than a simple infection. Do you have any other skin lesions elsewhere, and have you noticed any joint pain or eye redness recently?

text: My main symptom is Painful ulcerative lesion on the right leg. I also have Lesion has a central necrotic base and purplish irregular borders, History of ant bite at the site of the lesion, Pitting pedal edema of the lower extremities, Dilated tortuous veins in both lower legs.

speaker: Doctor
text: The description of a painful ulcer with a purplish, undermined border following minor trauma (pathergy) in a patient with Crohn's disease is highly suggestive of pyoderma gangrenosum, though the venous stasis signs complicate the picture. To confirm the diagnosis and rule out infection or vasculitis, I need to see the lesion directly. REQUEST IMAGES

speaker: Patient
text: Past medical history: ["Crohn's disease", 'Type 2 diabetes mellitus', 'Hypertension', 'Treated for anterior uveitis 8 months ago'] Social history: Recently returned from a visit to Wisconsin 2 months ago.

speaker: Doctor
text: The recent trip to Wisconsin raises the possibility of Sporotrichosis, but the purplish borders and pathergy strongly favor pyoderma gangrenosum. To rule out infection, I need a culture of the ulcer base. REQUEST TEST: Wound_Culture_and_Sensitivity

speaker: Doctor
text: The normal culture results and classic clinical presentation of a painful ulcer with purplish borders following minor trauma in a patient with Crohn's disease strongly point to a non-infectious etiology.
